headline: Sermorelin’s
missing approval.
dek: It was FDA approved as Geref. Both approvals were withdrawn in 2009.
byline: Adonis Men’s Health · Checked Oct 31, 2026 · Clinical review pending

glance.label: Approval withdrawn
glance.line: Geref approved 1990 and 1997; withdrawn June 18, 2009, at the maker’s request.

glance.label: Sleep trials
glance.line: No sermorelin trial with sleep as its result. Glycine: 3 small trials.

glance.label: Banned in sport
glance.line: Sermorelin is named under S2.2.4 and banned at all times. Glycine is not listed.

summary: [[/sermorelin|Sermorelin]] is a short version of growth hormone-releasing hormone, the signal that tells the pituitary to release growth hormone. It was once FDA approved, as Geref: in 1990 as a test of pituitary function and in 1997 for children with growth hormone deficiency. The maker stopped selling both products and asked FDA to withdraw them; FDA did, effective June 18, 2009. In 2013 FDA found they were not withdrawn for safety or effectiveness reasons. No sermorelin product is FDA approved today, so a product described as FDA approved is pointing to an approval that ended in 2009.

Compounded sermorelin, including troches, tablets, oral strips and injections, is not FDA approved, and using it for sleep or longevity is off-label. In 2022 a pharmacy recalled compounded sermorelin among other injectables for being out of specification. WADA names sermorelin under class S2.2.4 and bans it at all times.

The sleep research is indirect. We found no trial of sermorelin with sleep as its result, and no human study of sermorelin by mouth, troche or strip. In a 1999 German study of 23 men, natural GHRH given by nasal spray increased deep and REM sleep in the second half of the night; the abstract does not say whether it was sermorelin.

[[/glycine|Glycine]] is an amino acid sold as a dietary supplement and approved as a drug only as an irrigation fluid for urologic surgery. A 2026 scoping review found three small trials of glycine on sleep-related outcomes and called for larger ones. Whether glycine helps sleep, and whether sermorelin does at all, is not known.

excerpts.quote: The holders of the applications notified the agency in writing that the drug products were no longer marketed and requested that the approval of the applications be withdrawn. DATES: Effective: June 18, 2009.
excerpts.source: FDA, Withdrawal of approval of 92 NDAs and 49 ANDAs, Federal Register
excerpts.note: Geref Diagnostic (NDA 19-863) is on the notice’s list.

excerpts.quote: The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has determined that GEREF (Sermorelin Acetate) … were not withdrawn from sale for reasons of safety or effectiveness.
excerpts.source: FDA determination on GEREF, Federal Register
excerpts.note: The notice says this allows FDA to approve generic versions.

excerpts.quote: Olympia Pharmacy is voluntarily recalling 11 specific lots of Trimix Formulas F-9, T-105, SB-4, Sermorelin, Sincalide, Hydroxocobalamin, and NAD, compounded injectables to the consumer level. These compounded products were found to be out-of-specification.
excerpts.source: Olympia Pharmacy recall notice, posted by FDA

excerpts.quote: 1.5% Glycine Irrigation, USP is indicated for use as irrigating fluid during transurethral prostatic resection and other transurethral surgical procedures.
excerpts.note: This is glycine’s only FDA approval as a drug. It is not for sleep.

excerpts.quote: Moreover, results indicated that after intranasal administration GHRH increased rapid-eye-movement (REM) sleep and slow wave sleep (SWS), with this influence concentrating on the second half of sleep time.
excerpts.note: 12 young and 11 older healthy men, one night each. The abstract does not say whether the GHRH was sermorelin.

excerpts.quote: All 3 glycine sleep trials reported benefits on at least 1 sleep-related outcome.
excerpts.source: Fan et al., J Diet Suppl (scoping review)

excerpts.quote: Larger mechanistic trials with standardized sleep outcomes are needed.
excerpts.source: Fan et al., J Diet Suppl (scoping review)
